newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Kabul bombed as lull ends in Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: Kabul bombed as lull ends in Afghan war.

text.p: Warplanes dropped three bombs on Kabul on Thursday, apparently aiming for the airport, after a two-day lull in Afghanistan's latest war ended with an apparently successful ground attack by a northern alliance.
Witnesses said there were two air raids but the airport on the northeastern fringe of the city, used for both military and civilian traffic, appeared undamaged.
They said one bomb hit a mountainside next to the airport, but it was not clear where two more had landed in the midst of heavy anti-aircraft fire sent up by the Taleban defenders of the capital.

The purist Islamic Taleban militia, who conquered Kabul on September 27, also fired one ground-to-air missile but it did not appear to hit any of the planes, believed to belong to northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The air raids, about an hour apart, followed an apparently successful attack on Wednesday afternoon by the forces of Ahmad Shah Masood, the government military chief driven from Kabul a month ago, reliable sources said.
They said Masood, allied with Dostum, appeared to have broken a 10-day stalemate in fighting over a range of hills across the plain 25-30 km (15-19 miles) north of Kabul.
They said he sent a strong force down the western side of the valley around the flank of the Taleban lines, then swung east to take the village of Morad Beg, some 13 km (eight miles) from Kabul.

There was no immediate confirmation of the report because Taleban fighters manning a checkpoint at the top of the five km (three-mile) pass leading out of Kabul have refused to let Western reporters through for the past week.
Morad Beg is the last major village on the main road running down the valley into Kabul. Between the village and the city is a long stretch of gently undulating plain with few inhabitants.
The Taleban have stationed tanks, artillery and multiple rocket launchers along that stretch of road.

The sources said Masood's aim appeared to be to get behind the Taleban lines in the hills which have frustrated repeated attempts by Masood and Dostum to break through on the eastern side of the valley.
There, they have been trying to take the De Sabz pass, 30 km (19 miles) north of Kabul on the so-called new road that leads from there across sparsely populated terrain into northeastern Kabul.
Despite heavy fighting, the northern alliance has failed to dislodge the Taleban and Masood's flank attack appeared to have opened new possibilities, Afghan watchers said.

They said it was not clear whether the Taleban would move some of its hundreds of fighters from security duties in the capital to counter-attack against Masood or whether they would have to draw from elsewhere on the front line.
If they chose the second option, then Dostum's men might have a chance of capturing the De Sabz pass, they said.
The Taleban are also reported to be suffering reverses in the remote northwest, where they attacked Dostum directly for the first time, capturing Badghis province.
They had claimed to be pushing into neighbouring Faryab province, from which they could threaten Dostum's capital at Mazar-i-Sharif, but admitted implicitly on Wednesday they had been pushed back.
A Taleban spokesman quoted by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press reported heavy fighting in Badghis on Tuesday night.
Reliable sources in Kabul said Dostum had sent 2,000 men to meet the challenge on the new front and they had driven the Taleban almost back to the Badghis capital of Qalaye-i-Naw.
